Legends tell of sirens that lured sailors to the depths of the sea. But many other songs can be heard across the ocean. These sounds travel many hundreds of leagues in search of a familiar ear. For decades, scientists have tried to decipher whale's mysterious vocalisation and aspired to one day be able to access their wisdom. But as global warming has intensified the surface temperature of the Earth, sea levels across the planet have lowered to unprecedented levels. Now, formerly submerged seabed has given way to deserts of sun-scorched, glassy-bed salt sands. What remains of the oceans are limited to saltwater trenches running through the sands. The previously expansive broadcast area of whale calls has diminished. Where once hundreds of distinct calls and frequencies traversed hundreds of miles of ocean, comfortably crossing paths and separating from one another. The new, much narrower salt rivers now lead to signal interference. Crammed in ever smaller spaces... The whales struggle to communicate with each other clearly, leading to profound isolation. Unable to rely on their usual songs, they have turned, for the first time, to instruments. By grinding their bodies against driftwood and coconut husks, they create percussive rhythms over which their calves play fishbone xylophones using their teeth. They develop reed pipes from weeds and hollowed-out lobster claws. When the whales raise the pipes to their blowholes, they are often mistaken for periscopes of submarines navigating the salt rivers. But don't be fooled. This isn't a human-made machine, but an instrument in a natural orchestra. One that allows whales to communicate once again, both in the ocean channels and above the surface. Their songs can now sometimes be heard, ringing out across the vast, glassy bed deserts.
